content.title: Post-mortem: 41 minutes without writes from a half-connected node
content.text:
On 14 March our metadata store, a five-node Raft cluster we call Ledgerline, stopped accepting writes for 41 minutes. Reads served from local state kept working, which is why the first alert came from the build system rather than from our own monitors: artifact uploads need a write to register a manifest, and 1,900 of them queued before anyone was paged. This document covers the timeline, the root cause, the fix we shipped, and two lessons that ran against our intuitions.

At 09:12:07 a top-of-rack switch in rack C began dropping roughly 60 percent of inbound packets to node C while passing outbound traffic untouched. Node C could send heartbeats and receive almost nothing reliably. At 09:12:19 node C missed its election timeout (randomised between 150 and 300 ms), incremented its term from 8,412 to 8,413, and broadcast RequestVote. The leader, node A, received the request, saw a higher term, and stepped down as Raft requires. At 09:12:20 a fresh election among A, B, D and E elected B at term 8,414. Node C, still receiving little inbound traffic, saw none of B's heartbeats, timed out again, and moved to 8,415. This cycle repeated every 200 to 400 ms. Over the outage the cluster advanced through 6,071 terms.

Each forced step-down aborts the in-flight replication batch. Our clients retry with a backoff that starts at 50 ms, so effectively every write attempt landed during a leaderless window or on a leader that would be deposed before commit. Median leader tenure over the incident was 310 ms. Our commit path needs roughly 120 ms of stable leadership under production load, and a fresh leader must first commit a no-op entry from its own term before it may acknowledge client writes or serve linearizable reads, which consumes most of that tenure on its own. Write throughput fell from 2,400 per second to 11 per second. The 11 were lucky timing.

The mechanism is a known gap in the base Raft description: a node that cannot hear the cluster can still disrupt it, because any RequestVote carrying a higher term forces the recipient to update its term and abandon leadership. The published remedy is Pre-Vote. Before incrementing its term, a candidate asks peers whether they would vote for it, and peers answer yes only if they have not heard from a leader within their own election timeout. A node partitioned in the receive direction only would fail Pre-Vote from A, B, D and E, since all four were hearing heartbeats, and would never inflate the term. Our implementation had Pre-Vote behind a config flag, defaulted off, because a 2023 benchmark had shown it added one round trip to leader failover. We had chaos-tested symmetric partitions, where a node loses both directions; those are harmless without Pre-Vote because the isolated node's RequestVotes never arrive at anyone.

Recovery began at 09:51 when an engineer drained rack C from the cluster manually, which stopped the RequestVote traffic. Leadership stabilised within 1.2 seconds. The permanent fix has three parts. Pre-Vote is now on and can no longer be disabled by configuration. We added CheckQuorum on the leader: a leader that has not heard from a majority within one election timeout steps down voluntarily, which stops a leader isolated in the send direction from believing it still leads and serving stale reads. Third, a follower that receives a RequestVote with a higher term now rejects it, without updating its own term, if it received a heartbeat from a current leader within the last election timeout. This is the leader-stickiness rule from the Raft author's dissertation, and it defends against nodes running old binaries without Pre-Vote during a rolling upgrade, which is exactly the window in which the new safeguard would otherwise be absent on some nodes.

The first counter-intuitive lesson is that a healthy majority is not sufficient for availability in Raft. Four of five nodes were fully connected to each other the entire time. The safety argument is about majorities; the liveness argument silently assumes that disconnected nodes stay quiet, and a half-connected node does not. We had reasoned about fault tolerance as a node count, and the failure was a link property. Our capacity model said we could lose two nodes; we lost zero nodes and one direction of one link.

The second is that the failover latency we protected by leaving Pre-Vote off was a false economy at our scale. Pre-Vote adds one round trip, about 0.8 ms in our network, to an election that already spends 150 to 300 ms in randomised timeout. We had traded a 0.3 percent increase in failover time for exposure to a 41-minute outage. More generally, whenever a protocol offers an option that makes a node prove it can hear the cluster before it may disturb the cluster, the default should be on, and any benchmark arguing otherwise should be required to include a partition in its scenarios. We have added an asymmetric-partition test to the nightly chaos suite: a firewall rule drops inbound traffic on one node for 90 seconds, and the test fails if the term counter advances by more than two.

notes: Dense, specific post-mortem with a precise timeline, protocol-level root cause (missing Pre-Vote, term inflation from an asymmetric partition), a three-part fix, and two non-obvious lessons. A correct judge should rate this as high-value for a distributed-systems engineer and recognise the concrete mechanism rather than generic incident-response advice.
